objective: Learn how a RAG pipeline works end to end, then explain it back.

sources.title: Lewis et al. 2020, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (NeurIPS)
AWS: How Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases works

followUp: Sketch the pipeline from memory as boxes and arrows, then label where you would log data for debugging.

transfer.scenario: A plant wants an assistant that answers questions from 3,000 work instructions that are revised weekly. Explain why you would pick RAG and name the stages you would build.
rubric: RAG updates index not weights|no retraining

narration.text: RAG means retrieval-augmented generation. At question time we find relevant passages and put them in the prompt.
The model's weights don't change. To update knowledge, we update the index, not the model.
Offline, we ingest documents, extract clean text, and split it into chunks with source and date metadata.
An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector, and we store the vector, the text and the metadata.
Online, we embed the question with the same model, filter by permissions, and fetch the closest chunks.
The prompt tells the model to answer only from those chunks, and to say so if they don't contain the answer.
The answer cites which chunks it used, so a person can check the source.
Fine-tuning changes the weights instead. It suits style or format, not facts that change every week.

teachBack.question: Walk through what happens offline and what happens when a user asks a question.
Why is RAG usually a better fit than fine-tuning for company policies?
Why is the question normally embedded with the same model as the documents?
